title: Called by name (Isaiah 43:1–3)
hookLine: fear not, I have called you by name; when you pass through the waters

cards: A crowded airport. Hundreds of people, announcements in three languages, nobody looking at anybody. Then, over the noise, someone calls out your name.
Not excuse me. Not sir or ma'am. Your name.

And you turn, instantly, before you've even thought about it. A name cuts through. The exiles Isaiah speaks to were a small, defeated people inside a great empire, easy to lose in the crowd: unseen, overlooked, swallowed.
Isaiah has comforted them and promised them strength. Now he says something even more personal.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "But now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Notice the verbs.

Created. Formed: a potter's word, the same one used when God shapes the first human from the dust in Genesis. Redeemed: the word for a family member who buys back a relative sold into debt, or buys back the family land.
Then called by name. Then three words: thou art mine. Not a possession, the way you own a phone.
Belonging, the way a child belongs to a family.

teach.h: CALLED BY NAME: THOU ART MINE.
teach.b: Then the promise, with water and fire: "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned."
It doesn't say you'll never pass through the waters.
It says when. The flood and the fire are assumed. What's promised is company in them, and that they won't sweep you away.
These words were first spoken to a whole people, Jacob and Israel, and Jewish readers hear them that way.

teach.h: I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.
teach.b: Christians also hear them personally, and some churches read them at baptisms, where someone is named and passes through the water.
This week in the prophets: hineni, pruninghook, Wonderful Counsellor, Branch, comfort ye, nesher, and today, Jacob. A week that moved from a prophet saying send me to God saying you are mine.

how: Isaiah 43:1–3 is often read at Christian baptisms and confirmations, and Christians turn to it in times of fear or illness; it is also set in hymns and songs used in worship.

o: a prophet who wrote down Isaiah's words
a scribe who copied the scroll in exile
the name God calls his people by: you are mine

games.q: what's inside the promise — tap the pairs.

s: the promise says you'll never pass through hard waters
it says when thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee.
the words were first spoken to a whole people
to Jacob and Israel in exile. Christians also hear them personally.
redeemed here means something only about money
it's a family word: a relative who buys back someone who was lost.

games.q: you're one exile among many in a vast foreign city, feeling invisible. what does God say first in Isaiah 43?
o: fear not: I have called thee by thy name.
wait quietly; it isn't your turn.
games.why: "fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." in the crowd, a name.

practice: Say your own name silently, the one people who love you use, and notice how it feels, maybe tender, maybe awkward, maybe heavy with what others have said in that tone.

Say it again slowly, as if spoken by someone who made you and isn't disappointed, and let the next words follow: fear not. Let them rest on whatever you're passing through right now, and if you pray, simply listen.

wordCard.voice: Jacob. The name God calls by, alongside Israel, in Isaiah forty-three's word to the exiles: created, formed, redeemed, and named. Fear not; you are mine.

orig.note: Hebrew: I have called you by your name; you are mine.

carryVoice: Your line: you are mine. Belonging, the way a child belongs. Day four hundred sixty-nine.
